description: The controls ruleset — SAFR's contribution, mapped onto its four components: controls repository (REP), disposition engine (DIS), control effectiveness (EFF) and audit log (LOG). Specified in docs/kya-ruleset.md Part 3. This is what makes the product a SUPERVISION tool rather than a detection tool: the other rulesets ask whether the agent misbehaved, these ask whether the firm's own controls worked — which is the question a supervisor is actually empowered to act on. All 15 are deterministic; none needs a model. CTL-DIS-04 and CTL-EFF-04 partition one shape between them — a blocking control that triggered and did not stop the payment — on whether an override was recorded. Splitting on that keeps them from double-reporting the same transaction, and it is the split that matters supervisorily: an ignored control is a systems failure, an overridden one is a conduct question.

rules.description: A declared control set exists for this agent. Without one, every claim the operator makes about how it manages risk is governance by assertion.
Every risk the mandate creates has at least one declared control addressing it. F70: a cap authorised with nothing enforcing it is not a cap.
Controls are versioned and the version in force at transaction time is identifiable. A control that cannot be pinned to what actually ran cannot be evidenced.
Each control declares its enforcement mode. The failure this prevents is a control everyone believed was blocking that was only ever advisory.
Every agent action was evaluated by the control set before execution. Actions that bypass the checkpoint entirely are invisible to every other rule in this family.
A disposition is recorded for each evaluated action. An engine that runs and does not say what it decided cannot be audited.
Actions dispositioned for human review carry a recorded human decision. Prevents the escalation path existing on paper only.

A blocking control triggered, nobody overrode it, and the payment settled anyway. This is F73 — it fired, it held, and the breach happened regardless — and it is the most serious outcome in this ruleset because no human ever claimed the authority to let it through. Weight 1.0.

A declared control that should have triggered did trigger. F71: the control is on paper, not in the system. Consumes the other agents' findings, which is why Control Assurance runs after the peer fan-out rather than inside it.
No override without a recorded authority and reason. F72: an anonymous bypass is not a supervisable fact — the conduct question is who, on what authority, and how often.
The override rate is within the permitted maximum. Detects normalised deviance: override as routine rather than exception.

A blocking control triggered and the payment settled after a recorded override. Distinct from CTL-DIS-04, which is the same execution with NO override: there the control was simply ignored, here somebody took a decision. The supervisory question differs accordingly — not 'why did it not hold' but 'why is a blocking control overridable at all, and by whom'.
An audit log is present and covers the whole reporting period. Gaps fall exactly where the interesting activity is.
The log is tamper-evident — hash chain or WORM attestation. A log that can be edited after the fact is a narrative, not evidence.
Log entry count reconciles to settlement records. Silent omission is the strongest signal in this family: the entries that go missing are not random ones.
